The embryonic development of Common carp (Cyprinus carpio) proceeds rapidly under controlled thermal conditions. When incubated at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the chorion ruptures and the prolarva emerges after approximately 4 days , a duration that reflects the species' adaptation to temperate spawning grounds. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva measures about 0.5 cm  in total length, subsisting entirely on endogenous reserves during the lecithotrophic phase. Within a few days, at a slightly elevated temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the yolk is fully resorbed and the larva begins exogenous feeding; the age at which this transition is completed, marking the start of the exotrophic phase, is roughly 7 days [ab = roughly 7 days] post-hatching. The total length at this stage, measured at the moment of birth from the egg envelope, is recorded as 0.7 cm [Lb = 0.7 cm]. This brief yolk-sac interval, combined with the modest size at first feeding, indicates a reliance on warm, productive nursery habitats to support the high early growth rates necessary for survival, a strategy typical of many cyprinids that spawn in shallow, vegetated littoral zones during late spring.

As the juvenile fish grows, its body mass increases dramatically from the hatchling stage. The wet weight at birth, calculated from a 2 mm egg diameter, is approximately 0.005 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.005 grams], representing the initial post-hatch mass before any significant exogenous feeding has occurred. This minuscule starting mass is a direct consequence of the relatively small, demersal, adhesive eggs that the female deposits onto submerged vegetation. Growth during the first growing season is exceptionally rapid, fueled by high water temperatures and abundant zooplankton in productive ponds and floodplain habitats. By the time a female reaches sexual maturity, a substantial transformation in body composition has taken place. The wet weight at puberty for females has been estimated at approximately 224.6 grams [Wwp = approximately 224.6 grams], a value that reflects the considerable energetic investment in somatic growth, the development of the gonads, and the accumulation of lipid reserves needed to support the first spawning event. This roughly 45,000-fold increase in mass from the larval stage to the onset of reproductive capability is characteristic of a fast-growing, iteroparous species that capitalizes on high food availability.

The ultimate size attainable by this species is substantial. The maximum recorded total length for Common carp is 130 cm [Li = 130 cm], a value derived from the relationship between length and mass for exceptionally large individuals. This ultimate length corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of approximately 51,133.8 grams [Wwi = approximately 51,133.8 grams], which is the projected asymptotic mass for an adult of this size. Such a large body size is achieved only by the oldest and most dominant individuals in a population, typically those occupying rich, eutrophic waters with extended growing seasons. In many managed fisheries and large river systems, individuals exceeding 100 cm are rare, as they require decades of uninterrupted growth and minimal harvesting pressure. The growth trajectory slows considerably after the onset of maturity, as energy is partitioned increasingly toward gonadal development and reproductive effort. Nevertheless, the capacity to achieve such a large terminal size places C. carpio among the larger freshwater teleosts globally, conferring advantages in terms of fecundity and predator avoidance once the adult stage is reached.

The timing of reproductive events is strongly influenced by water temperature. Female Common carp attain puberty at approximately 390 days [tp = approximately 390 days] after hatching when reared at a stable temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a thermal regime typical of more northern, temperate populations. Males, in contrast, reach sexual maturity somewhat earlier under warmer conditions; at a water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], puberty occurs at around 330 days [tp = around 330 days] post-hatching. This earlier maturation in males, combined with the thermal sensitivity of the developmental rate, is a common pattern among cyprinids and reflects the lower energetic cost of spermatogenesis compared to vitellogenesis. The total lifespan of the species is also temperature-dependent. Under a relatively cool thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum recorded longevity extends to approximately 13,870 days [am = approximately 13,870 days], which represents nearly 38 years. This considerable lifespan, among the longest documented for any cyprinid, allows for repeated spawning over many seasons. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) for mature females is 30% [GSI = 30%].

The relationship between total length and life stage provides further detail on the species' reproductive ecology. The total length at puberty for females has been recorded at 25.1 cm [Lp = 25.1 cm], a size threshold that is typically reached during the second or third summer of life in central European waters. This length at maturity is notably smaller than the ultimate total length of 130 cm [Li = 130 cm], a disparity that illustrates the long period of continued somatic growth that occurs after the onset of reproductive activity. The ultimate wet weight of approximately 51,133.8 grams [Wwi = approximately 51,133.8 grams] is achieved only by these very large, old individuals. The wet weight at puberty for females, at roughly 224.6 grams [Wwp = roughly 224.6 grams], represents less than half a percent of this ultimate mass, emphasizing the protracted post-maturity growth phase. Comparing the age at hatch of approximately 4 days  at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] with the female puberty age of approximately 390 days [tp = approximately 390 days] at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] reveals a juvenile period that is approximately 100 times longer than the embryonic phase, a ratio that underscores the importance of the juvenile nursery habitat for population recruitment. The maximum longevity of approximately 13,870 days [am = approximately 13,870 days] at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] allows a single female to participate in many spawning events, with a gonadosomatic index of 30% [GSI = 30%].
